nameStory: The longhorn sculpin gets its name from the extra-long spines that project from its gill covers, looking like the horns of a longhorn cattle. These prominent spines are much longer than those of its cousin, the shorthorn sculpin, making this fish look like it's wearing nature's version of a spiked helmet.
description: The longhorn sculpin is a bottom-dwelling marine fish with a distinctive big head and tapering body that gives it a tadpole-like shape. These hardy fish typically grow to about 8-12 inches long and have a mottled brown and gray appearance that helps them blend perfectly with rocky seafloors. They're equipped with prominent spines and a large mouth, making them look like underwater gargoyles that patrol New England's coastal waters.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Large, flattened head that's wider than the narrow, tapering body - feels firm and bony to the touch with rough, sandpaper-like skin

idTips.label: Spines
idTips.description: Extra-long, sharp spines projecting from the gill covers that are notably longer than the fish's eye diameter - handle with care as they're needle-sharp

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Mottled brown, gray, and olive pattern with darker bands across the body that perfectly matches rocky bottom habitat

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Large, terminal mouth that opens wide with thick lips - big enough to engulf surprisingly large prey items

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Large, fan-like pectoral fins and two separate dorsal fins with the first having sharp spines that lock upright when threatened

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always found on or near rocky, pebbly, or shell-covered bottoms in cold marine waters, never in sandy areas

habitat: Longhorn sculpins live on rocky and pebbly bottoms of New England's coastal waters, from shallow tide pools down to depths of several hundred feet. They prefer areas with plenty of crevices and hiding spots among rocks, shells, and marine debris where they can ambush prey. You'll find them throughout the Gulf of Maine, around Cape Cod, and in deeper waters off southern New England.

seasonality.spring: Spawning occurs in late winter to early spring, when males may develop slightly brighter colors and become more territorial around rocky nesting sites.
seasonality.summer: Most active feeding season when they're easiest to spot hunting among tide pools and shallow rocky areas during low tide.
seasonality.fall: Begin moving to slightly deeper waters as temperatures drop, but remain active feeders preparing for winter.
seasonality.winter: Less active but still present in deeper rocky areas, often found by winter shore anglers fishing near structure.

funFact: Longhorn sculpins are nature's ultimate recyclers - they're such efficient scavengers that they'll eat almost anything that falls to the seafloor, including the molted shells of lobsters and crabs, making them the cleanup crew of New England's rocky reefs.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the shorthorn sculpin, but the longhorn's gill spines are dramatically longer - if the spine extends well beyond the eye diameter, you've got a longhorn. Memory trick: 'Long spines, longhorn' - the spines are so prominent they look like they could poke your eye out.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'sculpins,' these fish aren't closely related to freshwater sculpins found in New England streams. The name comes from their supposedly sculpted, artistic-looking head shape, though most people think they look more like underwater gargoyles than works of art.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the shorthorn sculpin, the longhorn has much more prominent gill spines and typically shows more distinct mottled patterning. The grubby sculpin, another relative, is much smaller and has a more compressed body shape with less prominent spines overall.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to the longhorn sculpin, the shorthorn has much shorter gill cover spines that don't extend past the gill edge.
Grubbies are much smaller than their relatives the shorthorn and longhorn sculpins, rarely exceeding 6 inches compared to their cousins' 12+ inch lengths.
